newsitem.title: UK: French franc retreats cautiously after budget.
newsitem.headline: French franc retreats cautiously after budget.

text.p: The French franc, buffeted by weeks of speculation about the credibility of the 1997 French budget, looks likely to return to calmer waters following the release on Wednesday of the government's fiscal plans.
The franc retreated just over one centime from a six-week high of 3.3957 francs per mark set on Tuesday following the official announcement of the extensively-leaked budget.

While economists expressed disquiet about the way the government has filled in budget holes to meet the deadlines for European economic and monetary union (EMU), traders said the franc's retreat was more a case of profit-taking following a one percent rally in the past two weeks.
"There is still concern about the way the French are plugging fiscal gaps and storing up problems down the road," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America.
"But, the franc's move this morning looks more like a case of buy the rumour/sell the fact," said Hawkins.
"Initially the market was very worried about the French budget, then it got very bullish and, now that it's out, things are just calming down a bit."
By 1400 GMT, the franc was trading at 3.4067 per mark, compared with 3.3982 late on Tuesday and its high during the day of 3.3957. Dollar/franc was at 5.1410 compared with 5.1457 late on Tuesday.
Some traders saw franc losses versus the more-buoyant dollar lately as hampering its strength against the mark as more and more people view the franc as a low-yielding, funding currency.
Others say franc weakness was exaggerated by options-related plays, while chartists saw strong support for the franc at 3.41 per mark and 5.16 per dollar.
"I think everyone would quite happy with mark/Paris about 3.40 and that will act as a bit of a pivot point now for while," said a senior trader at U.S. bank in London.

A Franco-German economic summit on Tuesday re-affirmed the committment in both countries to start EMU in 1999. And an EU finance ministers meeting in Dublin this weekend is expected to reach agreement on a post-EMU budget stability pact.
The French government's budget statement forecast a 1997 budget deficit of "below 3.0 percent" of gross domestic product, a number that will satisfy EMU target criteria.

The 1997 central government forecast was put at 283.7 billion francs ($55.07 billion), down from 288 billion in 1996, with a social security deficit of 30 billion francs, down from 50 billion this year. Without the recently announced tax reform package the deficit would have been 258 billion, the budget statement said.

While a deficit/GDP ratio of 3.0 percent would mean a nominal deficit of about 250 billion based on current government growth forecasts, a one-off payment to the state next year of 37.5 billion francs from French Telecom will fill the gap.

State bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC) is also expected to contribute 18 billion francs next year, while the welfare debt repayment fund CADES is expected to show a surplus in 1997 and also contribute.

"This has been so widely leaked beforehand it's hard to see any major reaction either way and the franc is likely hold up in this current weak-mark environment," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

"The French government is still playing two different games at the same time, however, and trying to keep its electoral chances alive while retaining market credibility in its EMU goals," said Lyons. ($1=5.151 French Franc)
